title: Explain OOP through all seven concepts (abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, composition, aggregation, association), and why OOP is important (modularity, maintainability, real-world modeling).
shortTitle: What are all seven OOP concepts?
keyPoints: Four pillars: encapsulation (protect), abstraction (simplify), inheritance (reuse), polymorphism (flex)
Association is the most general relationship: object A uses object B, both independent
Aggregation is weak HAS-A: parent has children, but children survive if parent is destroyed
Composition is strong OWNS-A: parent owns children, children are destroyed with parent
Together these seven concepts enable modularity, maintainability, and real-world modeling
In JPA: aggregation has no cascade delete, composition uses cascade ALL with orphanRemoval

s1_definition.oneliner: Four pillars (encapsulate, abstract, inherit, polymorph) plus three relationships (association, aggregation, composition) together enable modularity, maintainability, and real-world modeling.
s1_definition.profdef:
Beyond the four pillars, OOP includes three relationship concepts that describe how objects collaborate.

- **Association** is the most general relationship: object A uses object B, both exist independently (`TradeService` uses `NotificationService`).
- **Aggregation** is a weak HAS-A relationship: the parent has children, but children can exist independently (`Branch` has `Employee` objects that survive if the branch closes).
- **Composition** is a strong OWNS-A relationship: the parent owns children, and children cannot exist without the parent (`Account` owns `Transaction` records that are deleted when the account is closed).
- **Modularity** means each class is a self-contained unit that can be developed and tested independently.
- **Maintainability** means changing one class does not break others.
- **Real-world modeling** means bank accounts, trades, and customers map naturally to objects.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, all seven concepts coexist. Rajesh's account balance is private (encapsulation). Transfer hides 15 steps (abstraction). SavingsAccount extends Account (inheritance). calculateInterest() returns different results per type (polymorphism). TradeService uses MarketDataProvider (association). TradingDepartment has Traders who survive if the department closes (aggregation). Account owns Transactions that are deleted when the account closes (composition).

sections.s6_takeaway:
OOP has seven concepts: four pillars (encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism) and three relationship types (association, aggregation, composition). Association is the weakest: object A uses object B, both exist independently (SettlementService uses ClearingHouse). Aggregation is weak HAS-A: parent contains children but children survive if the parent is destroyed (TradingDepartment has Traders who move to another department when the desk is dissolved). Composition is strong OWNS-A: parent owns children, children are created by the parent and destroyed with it (Account owns Transactions that are deleted when the account is closed).

In Pankaj's banking architecture at National Bank of India, all seven concepts coexist in one system. SettlementService is associated with ClearingHouse through Spring dependency injection: replace the clearing house implementation and the settlement service continues unchanged. TradingDepartment aggregates Traders: dissolving the department returns the traders who can join a new department. Account composes Transactions: the deposit method creates transaction records that are permanently bound to the account and garbage collected when the account is closed. In JPA, composition maps to cascade ALL with orphanRemoval. Aggregation does not cascade deletes.

OOP matters because of three benefits: modularity (each class is a self-contained unit), maintainability (changing fee calculation requires zero changes to notification code), and real-world modeling (the code structure mirrors the banking domain).

Remember one sentence: four pillars build individual classes, three relationships connect them, and together they produce modular, maintainable software that mirrors the real world.
